lesson.title: Passphrases you can remember
lesson.subtitle: Why long beats complicated — and what never to share

video.title: Passphrases you can remember
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher (main character)
Ms Salma Haddad — secondary maths teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: Staff room, morning. Close-up of a phone showing a new-password box with three rules beside it: capital, number, symbol. Mr Okafor types; dots appear and each rule gets a tick. He leans back, proud, arms folded.
scenes.animation: Dots appear one by one; three ticks pop in 150 ms apart. Small push-in on his smile.
scenes.narration: A capital, a number, a symbol… my name, an at sign and my birth year. Same as my email and mobile money. Strong!
scenes.sound: Soft keyboard taps; light music bed starts.
scenes.vids: Flat phone illustration; show the password only as dots, never as text. Character: illustrated Grade 8 science teacher, ink outlines.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the lesson title and the cyber track chip with its icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: why long beats complicated — and how to make passwords you can actually remember.
scenes.vids: Use the Darsi title template (see brand kit). Keep the chip as icon + word.

scenes.visual: A simple box with a rolling counter stands for a guessing program. Guess cards fly past it: a football, a birthday cake, a name tag, then Mr Okafor’s dotted password card. The counter stops and his card flips over with a warning badge.
scenes.animation: Cards stream left to right, fast; counter digits roll. Warning badge pops (150 ms).
scenes.narration: Criminals don’t guess passwords by hand. Programs try millions of guesses — names, birthdays, football teams — and they know our tricks: a capital first, an at sign for “a”, a year at the end. That password is an easy guess.
scenes.sound: Fast ticking, then a soft buzz.
scenes.vids: Show the guessing program as a plain box with a counter, not a hooded hacker. Keep the cards free of readable text.

scenes.visual: Two padlocks side by side. The short one has three number dials and a counter that stops at 1,000. The long one has six dials; its counter rolls up to 1,000,000. One more dial slides onto the long padlock.
scenes.animation: Dials spin; the second counter rolls up quickly. The extra dial slides on with a click.
scenes.on_screen_text: Longer means far more to try
scenes.narration: What really slows a program down is length and surprise. A padlock with three dials has a thousand combinations. Six dials? A million. Every extra character multiplies the work.
scenes.sound: Dial clicks; rising tone as the counter climbs.
scenes.vids: Build the padlocks and dials with the Vids shape tools. Show the numbers as large, simple digits.

scenes.visual: Clean definition card on white with the cyber track chip. Three blank word cards drop into a row, then slide together and become one long key.
scenes.animation: Cards drop 300 ms apart, slide together and morph into a key shape.
scenes.narration: So here’s the idea: a passphrase. Pick three random words — words that have nothing to do with you or each other — and join them. Long, hard to guess and easy to picture. That’s the advice of the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre.
scenes.vids: Keep the card on screen for at least 6 seconds so teachers can read it in a second language.

scenes.visual: A thought bubble above Mr Okafor: a kettle full of mangoes sitting in a thunderstorm. He laughs. A pencil icon appears beside the bubble.
scenes.animation: Bubble pops open; one flat lightning bolt flashes once. The pencil wiggles.
scenes.narration: Kettle, mango, thunder. Picture a kettle full of mangoes in a thunderstorm — you won’t forget it. Don’t use ours, though: make your own.
scenes.sound: One soft thunder rumble, then a laugh.
scenes.vids: Flat illustration; no flashing faster than three times a second. The pencil reminds viewers to invent their own words.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma Haddad pops in with a raised eyebrow and a grin. Two answer cards drop in: a name tag with a cake and a symbol, and three small unrelated pictures in a row.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! Which would a guessing program crack first: a name with a year and a symbol, or three random words?
scenes.sound: Two gentle ‘pop’ sounds for the cards.
scenes.vids: The app pauses here (diamond marker). For the MP4 shared outside the app, hold this frame for 3 seconds with a small countdown ring.

scenes.visual: The name-tag card gets a warning badge and slides away. The three-pictures card gets a blue check badge and grows a little.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms). Quick 0.8 s confetti of three shapes in kola, sunbird and ink.
scenes.narration: The name, year and symbol — it’s short and predictable. Three random words are longer and much harder to guess.
scenes.vids: Use blue for correct (never green) and always pair it with the check icon.

scenes.visual: One key opens three doors: one with an envelope, one with a mobile money wallet, one with a chat bubble. A crack appears in the key and all the doors swing open. Rewind: each door gets its own key, and a notebook goes into a drawer at home.
scenes.animation: Doors swing open like dominoes; rewind wipe. New keys pop onto each door 200 ms apart.
scenes.narration: One password for everything is risky too. If one website leaks it, criminals try it everywhere. Email matters most — reset links go there. So give email and mobile money their own. Too many to remember? A written list, kept safe at home, beats reusing one password.
scenes.sound: Creaking doors; a light click for each key.
scenes.vids: Simple door shapes with icons on them; no real bank or app logos.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor’s phone buzzes with a code bubble shown as six dots. A caller silhouette on another phone asks for it. Mr Okafor raises an open hand and ends the call.
scenes.animation: Phone shakes once; the caller fades out as the call ends.
scenes.narration: And some things you never share: your password, your PIN, or a one-time code — the short code sent to your phone. No real bank or mobile money company will ask you to tell them these.
scenes.vids: Show the code as dots, never digits. Draw the caller as a neutral silhouette and avoid stereotyped ‘criminal’ imagery.

scenes.visual: A notice board with two old rule cards: one covered in symbols, one a calendar with every month circled. Both fade to grey and get a gentle cross. Beside them, a ruler grows longer next to a key.
scenes.animation: Cards fade to grey; a cross draws over each. The ruler extends smoothly.
scenes.narration: Two old rules you can let go: forcing symbols, and changing passwords every month. NIST, the US standards agency, tells organisations to allow long passwords and ask for a change only if one may have been stolen.
scenes.vids: Keep the crossed-out cards neutral grey so the new advice stands out in the cyber colour.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor holds his buzzing phone with a caller bubble on screen. Three answer cards bounce in: a mouth reading out dots, a phone hanging up beside a bank icon, a text bubble full of dots.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. A caller says he’s from my bank and wants the code just sent to my phone. What should I do?
scenes.vids: Second diamond marker — the app pauses for the question. In the MP4, hold for 3 seconds, then highlight ‘hang up and call the bank yourself’.

scenes.visual: The hang-up card gets the check badge. Then three summary cards line up: three small unrelated pictures, an envelope and a wallet each with its own key, and a raised open hand.
scenes.animation: Cards line up left to right, 250 ms apart.
scenes.narration: Hang up and call the bank yourself. Remember: three random words, a different passphrase for email and money, and never share a password, PIN or code.
scenes.vids: Hold the three cards for 5 seconds.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor’s classroom. A cloth bag of paper word cards passes along the rows. Pupils pull out three cards each and draw one funny picture linking them; one pupil holds hers up and the class laughs. End card: Darsi mark and ‘Next: Spot a phishing message’.
scenes.animation: Cards fly from the bag to pupils’ hands. End card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: put word cards in a bag. Pupils pull out three, draw one funny picture that links them, and see how easy a practice passphrase is to remember.
scenes.sound: Music resolves; no end jingle longer than 1 s.
scenes.vids: Classroom: illustrated pupils in local school uniforms; avoid stereotyped imagery. End card from the Darsi template.

checkpoints.prompt: Which would a guessing program crack first?

options.text: A name, a year and a symbol

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — names, years and the usual symbol swaps are among the first things guessing programs try.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — three random words are longer and less predictable. The name, year and symbol is the easier guess.

checkpoints.prompt: A “bank” caller wants the code just sent to your phone. What do you do?

options.text: Read the code out so they can help
Hang up and call the bank yourself
Send the code by text message instead

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a one-time code is yours alone. Call the bank on a number you already trust.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — anyone with that code could get into your account. Hang up and call the bank yourself.

video.vids_prompt: Create a 3 minute animated explainer video for teachers titled “Passphrases you can remember”. Style: flat, friendly illustration with bold ink outlines, light grey backgrounds, a tangerine (#ff6a2b) brand colour and hibiscus pink (#f04a7e); no gradients or blur. Main character: Mr Okafor, a Grade 8 science teacher. Follow the script scene by scene: a name-and-birth-year password that ticks every rule; guessing programs and padlock dials showing why length matters; three random words make a passphrase; separate passwords for email and mobile money; never share a password, PIN or one-time code; old rules about symbols and monthly changes; two quiz pauses; end with a word-card classroom activity. Use the narration exactly as written, a warm, calm voice, and keep on-screen text to six words or fewer per scene. No logos on screen.
